summary: The ustaz answers questions about the fate of the Prophet's parents and of people who never heard the call, holding to Allah's justice and mercy. He then explains how the Prophet SAW was protected in his youth from the shameless culture of Makkah, and connects it with the pornography and media challenges children face today. The second half presents shepherding as a leadership training module for the Prophet SAW: working for himself, patience, compassion, courage and strength, reflection and a simple life, and closes with the hadith that every one of us is a shepherd who will be asked.
keyPoints: Allah is Just and Merciful and does not punish anyone before a messenger reaches them, so the fate of those who never heard the call is left to Allah.
The Prophet SAW was protected by Allah from childhood from anything improper, even though he grew up in a society with little modesty in dress.
Parents need to be aware and check the data on pornography, music and media that expose children, starting with guarding themselves.
Shepherding was a leadership module for the prophets: earning by one's own effort, patience, compassion, courage and strength, reflection and a simple life.
The hadith that everyone is a shepherd makes leadership a responsibility that will be questioned, not a privilege.

chapters.title: Opening and the story of Hamka
chapters.summary: The lecture opens with Hamka's story of a young man returning from Makkah, before the ustaz recaps the previous episode.

chapters.title: The fate of the Prophet's parents and those who never heard the call
chapters.summary: With Surah Al-Isra, Ad-Duha and Fussilat, the ustaz shows Allah does not punish anyone before sending a messenger and is never unjust to His servants.

chapters.title: The hadith of the man who asked to be burned
chapters.summary: A Bukhari hadith about a man who despaired and was forgiven because he feared Allah, and the ustaz's conclusion on Allah's justice and mercy.

chapters.title: Correcting the infant mortality data
chapters.summary: The ustaz corrects the infant mortality figure he gave in Episode 6, from 50 percent to 15 percent in the 1950s.

chapters.title: Youth tested: singing, dancing and a culture without modesty
chapters.summary: The Prophet SAW grew up in a society that saw nudity as normal, and children played without an upper garment.

chapters.title: Youth without sabwah and the seven shaded by Allah
chapters.summary: Two hadith on the virtue of young people who guard themselves from deviation, and the Prophet SAW protected since childhood.

chapters.title: Hamka and the viral videos
chapters.summary: The ustaz is hurt by videos showing wrongdoing in Makkah and Madinah, and brings Hamka's polite but sharp reply.

chapters.title: Nudity, pornography and the data in Malaysia
chapters.summary: The ustaz presents data on access to pornography and the rise in sexual crimes against children, and what he learned from those working in the field.

chapters.title: Protecting children: music, cartoons and a hypersexual society
chapters.summary: Everyone is exposed, so awareness must rise about lyrics, music videos, drama, cartoons and sport.

chapters.title: Satan's agenda and checking the data
chapters.summary: Satan's first agenda was to strip away clothing and modesty. The ustaz also criticises religious talks full of crude jokes and reminds us that the sirah is about changing the status quo.

chapters.title: The Prophet SAW as a shepherd and hard work
chapters.summary: Several hadith on the prophets as shepherds, and the first lesson: the Prophet was trained to earn with his own hands.

chapters.title: Patience in guiding and mixing with people
chapters.summary: Shepherding trained patience and long vision, since sheep cannot see ahead, and a hadith on the believer who bears the harm of society.

chapters.title: Compassion, humility, courage and strength
chapters.summary: A shepherd does dirty work with compassion, and at the same time must be brave and strong against wild animals.

chapters.title: Reflection, minimalism and the circadian rhythm
chapters.summary: Shepherding gave time alone for tadabbur, a simple minimalist life, and alignment with the sun in the sunnah of sleep.

chapters.title: Every one of us is a shepherd who will be asked
chapters.summary: The hadith kullukum ra'in makes everyone responsible for their own flock, starting with the family.

chapters.title: Book and film recommendations
chapters.summary: The ustaz recommends the novel The Alchemist, the novel Hikmah Hati and the film The Goat Life as pictures of a shepherd's life.

lessons.title: Allah is Just and Merciful
lessons.body: The key to the fate of those who never received the call is Allah's justice and mercy, and He wrongs no one.

lessons.title: Focus on what affects us
lessons.body: There is no need to dwell on the fate of those who have passed. Everyone must think of themselves first.

lessons.title: Pray and strive
lessons.body: The Prophet SAW was protected by Allah, but he teaches us not only to pray but to strive to protect ourselves and our children.

lessons.title: Know the problem before fixing it
lessons.body: Parents must check the available data, because a problem cannot be solved if we do not know it exists.

lessons.title: Guard yourself first
lessons.body: Children see what we see and hear what we hear, so protecting them begins with protecting ourselves.

lessons.title: Religious talks need not use crude language
lessons.body: The Prophet SAW never used explicit language, and learning religion does not mean having no modesty.

lessons.title: Work and do not depend on handouts
lessons.body: The Prophet SAW was trained from childhood to earn by his own hard work, without a mindset of depending on others.

lessons.title: Patience in guiding people
lessons.body: A shepherd deals with all kinds of sheep and weather, which trains patience for guiding people who may also hurt you.

lessons.title: Compassion and humility
lessons.body: Doing the dirty work of caring for sheep softens the heart, and this compassion is why the prophets called their people Ya Qawmi.

lessons.title: Gentle but brave and strong
lessons.body: A shepherd's gentleness is not weakness, since he must be brave alone and strong against wild animals.

lessons.title: A simple life
lessons.body: Life in the desert taught the Prophet SAW to carry little, leaving him unattached to the world and able to endure hardship.

lessons.title: Align life with the sun
lessons.body: The prayer times and early sleep in the sunnah match the circadian rhythm, and research today supports the health benefits.

lessons.title: Leadership is a responsibility you will be asked about
lessons.body: The word mas'ul means responsibility that will be questioned, so everyone, beginning with the family, is a shepherd with a duty to perform.

lessons.title: Love for the Prophet SAW is shown by following him
lessons.body: Whatever we change should be out of love for the Prophet SAW, by following him in every aspect of life.

glossary.meaning: People who never received revelation or the call of a messenger; scholars discuss their fate at length.
Babies who die before the age of two; the ustaz corrects the 1950s figure to 150 per 1,000 births.
An inclination to deviate from the truth and do improper things.
Withdrawing to reflect, as the Prophet SAW did while shepherding.
Deep reflection, from the root dabara, meaning to see the meaning behind the words, not just read the surface.
Living with only the things that matter, including digital minimalism.
Full awareness, which the ustaz links to watchfulness and the sense that God is watching.
The body's biological clock that follows the sun, in line with the prayer times and sleep in the sunnah.
A shepherd, that is, one responsible for his flock, including leaders and heads of families.
One who is responsible and will be questioned, not a term of privilege or honour.

dalil.context: No one bears another's burden of sin, and Allah does not punish anyone until He has sent a messenger to make clear right and wrong.
dalil.translation: Whoever accepts guidance does so for his own good; whoever strays does so at his own peril. No soul will bear another’s burden, nor do We punish until We have sent a messenger.

dalil.context: Prof. Quraish Shihab quotes this verse in his book as comfort for the Prophet SAW, which may also have eased his worry about his parents.
dalil.translation: your Lord is sure to give you so much that you will be well satisfied.

dalil.context: Allah is never unjust to His servants, one of the ustaz's keys for thinking about those who never received the call.
dalil.translation: Whoever does good does it for his own soul and whoever does evil does it against his own soul: your Lord is never unjust to His creatures.

dalil.context: Scholars discuss whether the man's act was disbelief, but Allah forgave him because he feared Him. The ustaz holds to Allah's justice and mercy here.
dalil.translation: A man who had transgressed against himself despaired of his sins. He told his children that when he died they should burn him, crush him to dust and scatter him so the wind would carry him away. He said, by Allah, if my Lord catches me He will punish me with a punishment He has never given anyone. Allah gathered him again and asked why he had done it. He answered, only out of fear of You, and Allah forgave him.

dalil.context: The ustaz brings this hadith to show the Prophet SAW was protected by Allah from childhood from deviation, and there is no record of him doing it.
dalil.translation: Your Lord is amazed by a young man who has no sabwah, that is, no inclination to deviate from the truth and do improper things.

dalil.context: The ustaz pictures the hot gathering ground and people drenched in sweat, while these seven sit in comfort. The hadith is linked to the merit of young people who guard themselves.
dalil.translation: Seven will be shaded by Allah on the day when there is no shade but His. One of them is the young man who grew up in worship and obedience to Allah.

dalil.context: According to one narration the ustaz mentions, the Prophet SAW became a shepherd after moving to Abu Talib's house at the age of eight.
dalil.translation: Allah did not send a prophet except that he was a shepherd of sheep. The Companions asked, and you too, O Messenger of Allah? He said, yes, I herded sheep for the people of Makkah for a few coins.

dalil.context: The ustaz mentions Ajyad as an area in Makkah that people who go for umrah will know.
dalil.translation: Musa was sent and he was once a shepherd. Dawud was sent and he was also a shepherd. I too once herded sheep at Ajyad.

dalil.context: The ustaz stresses working independently and reminds us that provision is about moving, not just sitting in worship.
dalil.translation: No one has ever eaten better food than that which comes from the work of his own hands.

dalil.context: The better person is the one who earns a living through his own hard work.
dalil.translation: A man who goes out, cuts firewood and carries it on his back is better than a man who begs, whether he is given or refused.

dalil.context: The ustaz reminds himself of this hadith when he feels lazy about calling to Allah because he is still criticised. Every prophet suffered, and the Prophet SAW comforted himself with the story of Musa's people.
dalil.translation: The believer who mixes with people and bears the harm they cause is better than the believer who does not mix with people and does not bear their harm.

dalil.context: The ustaz stresses this hadith names sheep specifically, not camels, horses or cattle, and that dirty work softens the heart.
dalil.translation: Arrogance and pride belong to those who herd camels, while calm and gentleness belong to those who herd sheep.

dalil.context: The ustaz brings this narration to show the Prophet SAW's very simple life, the result of his training as a shepherd.
dalil.translation: Umar al-Khattab wept when he saw the marks of the mat on the Prophet SAW's body as he got up, and said the kings of Persia and Rome live in comfort while the Messenger of Allah sleeps on a mat. The Prophet replied, are you not pleased, Umar, that they have this world and we have the Hereafter?

dalil.context: The ustaz says research today shows the harm of sleeping on the stomach, and that much of the sunnah on sleep matches the circadian rhythm.
dalil.translation: Sleeping on the stomach is the way Satan sleeps.

dalil.context: The ustaz stresses the Arabic word is mas'ul, a responsibility that will be questioned, not a privilege or honour.
dalil.translation: All of you are shepherds, and all of you will be asked about your flock. A leader is asked about his people, a man about his wife and children, a woman about her children and her husband's home, and a servant about the property and trust given to him.
